work.title: Liber de Unico Baptismo

paragraphs.text: Brother Constantine, we are very often compelled to answer those who hold different views and stray from the rule of truth, even on matters we have dealt with again and again in one discourse after another. I think this is useful for two reasons. The first is the slower wits of those who think something different is being said when they read the same thing put in a different way. The second is the very abundance of such disputations: the matter should not reach only the diligent, as something rare, but one or another of many writings may fall into the hands even of the more careless. You gave me a treatise On the One Baptism, composed by those who repeat baptism, which you had received from some presbyter or other of the Donatists when we were together in the country, and you earnestly asked me to answer it. It is puffed up with nothing but a din of words and made harsh with slanderous accusations. See, with the Lord's help, how easily I refute it.

The first grievance raised there is that a secret matter is being aired in public. Then let those who think this ought not to be done keep silent. Or if they say they are compelled to speak in order to answer those who think otherwise, this is our case too: we answer not only those who think otherwise but also those who act otherwise. For what does harm in secret must be refuted openly, since it is also defended openly when people are being persuaded, so that it may do harm in secret when it is carried out. For who baptizes anyone in the presence of the uninitiated? And yet no uninitiated person is unaware that Christians are baptized, for he hears in public what he may receive in secret if he believes.

Let us see, then, what they say about repeating baptism, these men who are ashamed to say openly what I wish they were afraid to commit openly. "The question," he says, "is where true baptism is to be found." Then he adds: "So truly is it mine that what I have given once is not repeated even by the sacrilegious themselves." To him we reply: the man who does not dare to repeat the one baptism, which is not yours but Christ's, is not sacrilegious. For the single consecration of a person in baptism belongs to Christ, but the repetition of the one baptism belongs to you. I correct in you what is yours; I acknowledge what is Christ's. For this is just: when we condemn the evils of men, we should approve whatever good things of God we find in them. This, I say, is just: that even in a sacrilegious man I should not violate what I find to be a true sacrament, lest in amending the sacrilegious man I commit sacrilege in his person.

For these men are evil in a good baptism, just as the Jews are evil in a good law. And so, as the Jews will be judged by the very law which their wickedness did not make evil, so these men too will be judged by the very baptism which they, being evil, have held though it is good. Therefore, when a Jew comes to us to become a Christian, we do not destroy the good things of God in him, but his own evils. He errs in not believing that Christ has already come, been born, suffered and risen: this we correct, and having destroyed that unbelief, we build up the faith by which these things are believed. Likewise he errs in clinging to the shadows of the old sacraments: from this we dissuade him, and we show that the time has now come when, as the prophets foretold, these things were to be taken away and changed. But that he believes that the one God who made heaven and earth is to be worshiped, that he detests all the idols and sacrileges of the Gentiles, that he awaits the judgment to come, that he hopes for eternal life, that he does not doubt the resurrection of the flesh — all this we praise, approve and acknowledge; as he believed what is to be believed and held what is to be held, so we confirm it. In the same way, when a schismatic or heretic comes to us to become a Catholic, we cut away his schism and heresy by dissuading him from them and destroying them. But the Christian sacraments, if we find them unaltered in him, and whatever else that is true he holds — far be it from us to violate them; far be it from us to repeat what we know is to be given once, lest, while we cure human faults, we condemn divine remedies, or, by seeking to heal what is not wounded, we wound the man where he is sound. Accordingly, if I find a heretic who dissents on some matter belonging to the Christian and Catholic faith, even on the very unity of the Trinity, and yet has been baptized according to the rule of the gospel and the Church, I correct the man's understanding; I do not violate God's sacrament. I am speaking of Jews, and of schismatics or heretics who err under the name of Christ in whatever way.

As for the Gentiles themselves and the worshipers of idols, who are certainly far removed from us by many differences, the apostle shows us nothing other than this: that in them too we should correct whatever is perverse in such a way that we approve whatever may happen to be right. For he was certainly rebuking idolaters — and, what is more serious, not only the worshipers of images but their very founders — when he said: Who, knowing God, did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man and of birds and four-footed beasts and serpents. Such, we know, were the images of the Egyptians, where an idolatry more manifold and far more shameful is said to have been established. Yet did he deny that there was knowledge of God in them? Did he not rather confirm it, saying: Knowing God, they did not glorify him as God? If, then, he had tried to refute and destroy this knowledge as a lie because he had found it in sacrilegious men, would he not — God forbid — have shown himself an enemy of the truth? So he blames, detests and overthrows what they changed into their own lie. For here too he said: They exchanged the glory of God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man — that is, imagining God to be what God is not, and not handing him on to men as they had known him. And a little later he says of such people: Who exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. For the truth about the creature, that it comes from God and is not God, they turned into a lie, worshiping as gods the sun and moon and whatever is in heaven and on earth. What they changed into their own lie, then, he blames, detests and overthrows; but whatever truth they preserved in a teaching mixed and confused with many falsehoods, he approves, attests and affirms. For here too he began the same passage by saying: For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of those men who hold down the truth in unrighteousness. He does not deny the truth, even though it is held down in unrighteous-

ness. And in the Acts of the Apostles, when he was teaching the Athenians about the one true God, that in him we live and move and have our being, he at once added: As some of your own have said. This, then — that in God we live and move and have our being — comes from that truth which even those ungodly worshipers of images hold down in unrighteousness, who, knowing God, did not glorify him as God. Yet this truth, found, as we see, among the ungodly and sacrilegious, the apostle does not destroy but confirms, and he uses its testimony to teach those who did not know these things. Bishop Cyprian followed this apostolic rule. When he argued about the one true God against the worshipers of many false gods, he brought forward many testimonies from the books of those whom they regard as distinguished authors, that is, from that truth which they hold down in unrighteousness. But what the apostle did is far more remarkable. Going round their shrines, he found among the altars of demons a certain altar on which was written, To an unknown god. He did not destroy this by denying and refuting it; rather, by confirming it, he found in it the most fitting opening for his discourse, saying: Him whom you worship without knowing, him I proclaim to you.

We, therefore, follow this apostolic rule, handed down to us through our forebears. If we find anything right even in the perverse, we correct their perversity but in no way violate what is right, so that in one and the same man the false things are amended by means of the true things he holds, and the true things are not destroyed along with the falsehoods that have been refuted. In the time of the apostles, those who said, I am of Paul, I of Apollos, I of Cephas, were themselves making ungodly schisms, even though they did so not under the names of the ungodly but of saints. This was their own detestable fault. But that they knew Christ had been crucified for them and that they had been baptized in his name did not come from their error but from God's gift among them; this truth of God they held down in the unrighteousness of their schisms. The most blessed Paul seized on this truth. He did not destroy it when he destroyed those faults; rather, by confirming it he showed that those faults had to be amended — Was Paul crucified for you, he says, or were you baptized in the name of Paul? — so that through the truth of God which they held they might blush at the falsehood of their own which they practiced. So it is said to a Jew: "Hold the faith in the resurrection of the dead as you held it, but now believe what you did not believe, that Christ has risen from the dead. For you hold down God's truth about the resurrection of the dead in your unrighteousness, in which you do not believe that Christ has risen." So it is said to a worshiper of idols: "Hold what you held, that the world was founded by the one true God, but do not believe that pieces of wood and stone are gods, or whatever parts of the world itself you used to worship. For you hold down the truth of God, by which you believe the world was founded by him, in your unrighteousness, by which you choose to be a worshiper of false gods." In the same way it is said to a heretic who has altered by no falsehood of his own the Christian sacraments as they are handed down in the Catholic Church: "Hold Christian baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit as you held it, but acknowledge the Church of Christ, growing, as was prophesied, throughout the whole world, which you used to curse with a sacrilegious voice. For you hold down God's truth about the oneness of baptism in the unrighteousness of your division. Correct the unrighteousness of your heretical invention, lest it destroy you, and do not be proud of the truth of the Christian sacrament, which is there to judge you. But far be it from me so to detest your unrighteousness as to deny the truth of Christ, which I find in you to your condemnation; far be it from me so to correct you as to destroy the very thing by which I correct you. Or perhaps I ought to destroy the truth I find in the soul of heretics, when the apostle did not destroy the truth he found on the stone of pagans?"

The one God is greater than the one baptism. For baptism is not God; it is something great precisely because it is a sacrament of God. And yet this one God was worshiped even outside the Church by those who did not know him. In the same way, then, the one baptism too is given even outside the Church by those who do not know. Whoever says it was impossible for the one true God to be worshiped outside the Church by those who did not know him, let him consider what answer he can give, not to me, but to the apostle himself, who says: Him whom you worship without knowing, him I proclaim to you.

Worshiping the true God without knowing him did nothing for the salvation of those who did it. Indeed, it even contributed to their ruin, since by worshiping false gods at the same time they did sacrilegious injury to that same true God. In the same way, it does nothing for the salvation of heretics that outside the Church, through ignorance, they both hand on and hold true baptism. Indeed, it even contributes to their condemnation, since in the sacrilegious unrighteousness of human error they hold down the truth even of a divine sacrament, not so as to be cleansed by it, but so as to be judged by it more severely. And when the apostle was correcting those sacrilegious men, he nevertheless acknowledged rather than denied the true God whom they worshiped outside the Church without knowing him. So we too, when we correct the errors of heretics in their sacrilegious separation, ought certainly to acknowledge, not deny, the true baptism which they hand on outside the Church through ignorance.

"But," they say, "when Paul came to Ephesus, he ordered certain men who said they had been baptized with John's baptism to be baptized in Christ." Whoever thinks on the strength of this example that schismatics and heretics must be baptized, let him dare to say, if he can, that John was a heretic or a schismatic. If it is wicked to say this, then surely those men were given what they lacked, and what they already had was not condemned. This holds whether they lied in claiming to have John's baptism, as some suppose, or whether it was because John's baptism was not the baptism of Christ, though it did serve Christ, just as the ancient sacraments of the Law performed a kind of forerunning and prefiguring function. "But," they say, "if people were baptized after John, the friend of the bridegroom, how much more must they be baptized after a heretic!" Someone else, stirred by what seems a similarly just indignation, could say: "If people were baptized after John, who drank no wine at all, how much more justly must they be baptized after a drunkard! So let these people do this, if they can: let them baptize after their own drunkards, since the apostles baptized after the sober John." What do they answer to this, except that they do not baptize after such men because those who were baptized by them received not their baptism but Christ's? Let them believe, then, that people were baptized after John because those men either had no baptism at all or did not yet have the baptism of Christ.

Indeed, the very man we are answering raised this objection against himself too, and once he had raised it he did not resolve it. For he says: "Perhaps someone will say: 'But those whom Paul baptized again had been washed with the baptism of John, not with the baptism of Jesus Christ. Hence I say that those who are known to have been baptized by traditors, but nevertheless in the name of Christ, ought not to be rebaptized.'" Having put this to himself, notice how vainly he tried to answer it. "To this matter," he says, "the Lord Christ responded with these words: 'Whoever does not gather with me scatters'; and again: 'Not everyone who says to me, "Lord, Lord," will enter the kingdom of heaven. For many will say to me on that day, "Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?" And then I will say to them, "I do not know you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity."' There is no doubt, then, that those who dared to act as sacrilegious men, even though in the name of Jesus Christ, have lost their false work. Whether they like it or not, the traditors therefore offend Christ all the more with their sacrilegious sacraments; and if they dare to say, 'We prophesied in your name,' he will say to them as to the rest: 'Depart from me, you workers of iniquity; I do not know you.' He will rightly say this to them, since in the unworthy, baptizing, driving out demons and performing other wonderful mighty works are not dissimilar cases." See how much he said, and yet he could not resolve at all the objection he had posed against himself. Not only did he fail to resolve it; he even reminded us of what we ought to say against them. For these testimonies from the gospel not only do nothing to help him, but they even give strong support to our case.

The question was about the baptism of John. If the apostle baptized certain men who had been baptized by John, he certainly did not give John's baptism a second time to men who already had John's baptism. Rather, he ordered men who did not have the baptism of Christ to be baptized in Christ, and in doing so he destroyed neither baptism but distinguished the two. The man we are arguing against saw this too. He raised against himself, as if from his opponents' side, the objection that those whom they call traditors also baptize and are baptized with the baptism of Christ, not of John, and that therefore their baptism ought neither to be annulled nor repeated. He said that Christ had answered this question when he said, "Whoever does not gather with me scatters," as though Christ had said: "In those who do not gather with me, even what is found to be true and to be mine must be denied, exorcised and destroyed." He also said that to certain people who say, "Lord, Lord, did we not prophesy in your name, and cast out demons in your name, and do many mighty works in your name?" the Lord will answer: "I do not know you; depart from me, you who work iniquity." Did he say here too: "Because of your iniquity I will deny even my own truth, which is held captive in your iniquity"? For he will not receive into his kingdom all in whom he finds some truth, but those in whom he finds the love that befits the truth. Where that love is lacking there will be iniquity; yet the truth held captive in that iniquity must not be denied. Rather, the iniquity itself must be condemned, without destroying the truth. Hence the apostle too says: "Even if I know all mysteries and all knowledge, and even if I have all prophecy and all faith, so that I can move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing." He said that he himself would be nothing if he did not have love, not that the mysteries and knowledge and prophecy and faith would be nothing. For these things are great, even if the man who has them without love, and holds their truth captive in his own iniquity, is nothing. This is what we too say to these heretics: "We do not destroy the truth of baptism which you hold captive in your iniquity; but when we correct you, we destroy and overturn your iniquity, while we recognize and hold fast to the truth." So these further testimonies from the gospel are of no help to him at all.

Now notice how they actually give us strong support. Look closely at his own words: "There is no doubt," he says, "that those who dared to act as sacrilegious men, even though in the name of Jesus Christ, have lost their false work." This is entirely true, for those who as sacrilegious men dared to act in the name of Jesus Christ have lost their own false work. But does that make the very name of Jesus Christ sacrilegious, even when sacrilegious men do something by it? Who, even the most demented, would dare to say this? What pagan, at this point in time, would dare to assert it? Hence Jesus Christ himself, though he said with perfect truth, "Whoever does not gather with me scatters," nevertheless, when his disciples told him that they had found someone casting out demons in his name and had forbidden him because he did not follow the Lord with them, answered: "Do not forbid him; for no one does mighty works in my name and can then speak evil of me." Certainly that man had his own iniquity, in that he was not gathering with the Lord and was not following the Shepherd with the disciples in the unity of his flock. In that iniquity of his he held captive a truth that was not his own, namely that he cast out demons in the name of Jesus Christ and did not speak evil of him. So the Lord condemns this man's iniquity in the words "Whoever does not gather with me scatters"; yet he neither denies nor rejects his own truth in him when he says, "Do not forbid him; for no one does mighty works in my name and can then speak evil of me." Following this example of the Lord as far as we are able, we too cannot deny the truth of baptism, or anything else true that the heretics hold, and we do not dare to reject or destroy it. But we rightly detest their own iniquity, by which they do not gather with Christ but scatter; and while leaving untouched the truth that is in them, we condemn that iniquity, or correct it as far as we are allowed.

Let him see clearly, then, how mistaken he was in what he went on to add: "Whether they like it or not, the traditors therefore offend Christ all the more with their sacrilegious sacraments." It is one piece of rashness, though tolerable after a fashion, that he calls men traditors without proving that they are. But who could put up with his calling the sacraments of Christ sacrilegious, sacraments that are celebrated in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit according to the rite of the gospel, even if they really were held by traditors, as he slanderously claims? Here perhaps he might say that what is given by sacrilegious men is no longer a sacrament of Christ. Why then does he not also say that what is spoken by sacrilegious men is not the name of Christ? That he certainly did not dare to say. For he says: "There is no doubt, then, that those who dared to act as sacrilegious men, even though in the name of Jesus Christ, have lost their false work." "Even though in the name of Jesus Christ," he says. Did he say that it was not the name of Jesus Christ? Just as it does sacrilegious men no good that they act in the name of Jesus Christ, so it does heretics no good that they baptize or are baptized with the baptism of Jesus Christ. And yet, just as that name is the name of Jesus Christ, so this baptism is the baptism of Jesus Christ; and both must be recognized and approved, not denied and destroyed, so that no injury is done to such great gifts of God while the lives of sacrilegious men who misuse these good things are being corrected.

He says that the Lord will say "Depart from me, you who work iniquity" to sacrilegious men who outside the Church baptize, or cast out demons, or perform other mighty works in the name of Jesus Christ. We, however, say—or rather the truth itself says—that the Lord will say this to all such people, including those who swim as bad fish among the good within the very nets of unity, right up to the shore. For when the good have been gathered into the vessels and the bad have been separated and thrown away, what else will be said to them but "Depart from me, you who work iniquity"? And yet we do not destroy the sacraments of Christ in them, since we recognize both those who baptize and those who are baptized, such as they are, within the same nets of unity. Nor do I think that they themselves are so shameless as to dare to say that the Lord will not say "Depart from me, you who work iniquity" to the very many wicked and criminal people on their side who are ruined and defiled by open disgraces and crimes: the greedy and the plunderers, the ruthless usurers and the bloodthirsty Circumcellions. And yet they know, they see, they are certain that many such men baptize and that many are baptized by such men; and even those among them who are displeased by these men's crimes do not violate the sacrament of Christ in them. So not only did he say nothing against us when he brought forward these testimonies from the gospel; he even reminded us of what we should say against them.

Accordingly, in what follows he says exultantly, "I have briefly resolved the question." He has indeed resolved it, but in our favor. He says that in the unworthy, baptizing, driving out demons and performing other mighty works are not dissimilar cases, and that to those who say, "We did these things in your name," the Lord will say, "I do not know you; depart from me, you workers of iniquity." In saying this he has made it plain that it is just as true that those who are separated from the Church baptize with the baptism of Jesus Christ as it is true that they drive out demons in the name of Jesus Christ, but that neither of these brings them to eternal life or rescues them from eternal punishment. The disciples saw a man who was separated from the flock of Jesus Christ driving out demons in the name of Jesus Christ. Suppose one of those from whom he had driven out demons came to the Church: the mighty work that had been done in him would in no way be denied, but what he lacked would be added. In the same way, when anyone who has been consecrated outside the Church by heretics or schismatics, yet with the baptism of Christ, comes to the Church, the sacrament of truth with which he was imbued must not be denied. What must be added is the devotion of unity, from which he was separated, and without which that sacrament could be present in him but could not profit him. This is what we do; this is what we have received as handed down by our forebears; this is what we guard in the Catholic Church, which is spread throughout the whole world, against all the fogs of falsehood. What more, then, need we argue on this point, since he himself has briefly resolved the question by citing testimonies from the gospel? Surely, if he did not want to be contentious, he would use them both to condemn his own error and to recognize the truth of baptism.

Why, then, is there any need to go back over all his words, in which he thinks he is arguing cleverly, turning over at great length the claim that true baptism is on his side because it is recognized, not denied, by us as well? For whoever holds firm and unshaken what the most true and inviolable rule of truth shows—that in each person whatever is false and corrupt must be rejected or corrected, while whatever is true and right must be recognized and accepted—sees at once both what we detest in the heresy of the Donatists and what we must by no means violate. For since they hold the truth of baptism captive in the iniquity of their separation, we find fault with their iniquity, but the truth of baptism is recognized and approved everywhere.

For whoever says that the baptism of Christ must be destroyed when heretics baptize with it must logically say that Christ himself must be denied when demons confess him. Peter was praised for saying, "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God"; the demons were driven out though they said the very same thing: "We know who you are, the Son of God." So this confession was fruitful for Peter and ruinous for the demons, yet in both cases it is not false but true; it must not be denied but recognized, not detested but approved. So too the truth of baptism is given by upright Catholics as that confession was given by Peter, and it is given by perverse heretics as the same confession was given by the demons. It helps the former and condemns the latter; yet in both it must be approved by being recognized, and in neither must it be violated by being denied. Hence the apostle James too, when he rebuked certain people who said that true faith was enough for a man and did not join to it the works of love, refuted them by this very comparison with the demons, so that they would not imagine that they belonged to God because they believed what was true about God, even if they did not trouble to add good works to their faith. "You believe," he says, "that God is one? You do well; the demons also believe, and tremble." So he compared those who believe what is true about God but live wickedly to demons; yet he did not deny and destroy that very truth which the demons believe about God, out of hatred for the demons. Therefore, since the very man we are arguing against has cited the apostle as saying, "One God, one faith, one baptism," consider: we find the same God worshiped outside the Church by those who do not know him; we find the same faith in the one God confessed outside the Church not only by certain men but even by demons; and yet both were confirmed by the apostles rather than denied. Why, then, do we not likewise confirm rather than deny the one baptism in those we find established outside the Church? In this way we will not corrupt what is right in them because of what is crooked in them, but rather, starting from the right thing they hold, correct the very thing in which they have been corrupted.

What, then, does he mean when he says that true baptism is there where true faith is? It is perfectly possible for some to have true baptism and not have true faith, just as it is possible for them to have the true gospel and yet, by not understanding it rightly, to believe something false about God. Shall we think, because of that falsity in their faith, that the gospel too, which is found to be true among them, must be detested or corrected? Nor do I think that those Corinthians whom the apostle rebuked for splitting into schisms had true faith in saying, "I belong to Paul"; for this was false. Yet they had true baptism, and it was from its truth that they heard from the apostle himself, in order to correct that falsehood: "Was Paul crucified for you, or were you baptized in the name of Paul?" There were also people there who did not believe that the dead rise, and in this they certainly did not hold or have true faith. Yet starting from the truth they did have—since they believed that Christ, in whom they had been baptized, had risen—the apostle strives to heal also the point in which their faith was not sound, saying: "If the dead do not rise, then Christ has not risen either." In this way, since they had believed that Christ had risen and this was sound in them, the other point might also be healed, namely that through a most ruinous error they did not believe that the dead rise. So, in the holy canonical Scriptures, they do not find heretics coming to the Catholic Church being baptized again, nor do we find them being received in the same baptism they had received in heresy. On this point, at least, our case is equal: neither what they do, in baptizing again heretics or those they consider heretics, nor what we do, in accepting the baptism of Christ even when it has been given among heretics, is confirmed by any explicit example from the apostolic age. But we find that the apostles, in people who were in any kind of error or sacrilegious through any kind of impiety, confirmed rather than denied whatever truth those people knew, while they corrected or condemned their error and impiety without harm to what was found true in them. We follow this rule also with respect to the truth of baptism. Wherever we find it retained and preserved just as it is retained and preserved in the Catholic Church, we do not deny or destroy it; rather, while it remains intact, we treat, correct and amend whatever is corrupt, crooked or false in each person, or, if we cannot, we detest it, condemn it and shun it.

Accordingly, when we receive them, we do not receive their iniquity, by which they have divided themselves from the Church of Christ in a sacrilegious rupture, and by which they assail with slanderous and abusive accusations the Christian world, to which God bears so many testimonies through the Law, through the prophets, through the gospel, through the psalms, through the apostles. Nor do we receive that error of theirs by which they refuse to recognize the baptism of Christ even when it is kept among heretics according to the rule of the Church, by which they dare to destroy it and do not hesitate to repeat it. Indeed, if they manage by some means to lead astray and win over to themselves not only laypeople but also clergy—and not just any clergy, but even presbyters and bishops—they make them catechumens, even if they were baptized in those churches which the apostles themselves founded by their own labor. These detestable evils of theirs we by no means receive, since they cannot cross over to us unless these have been corrected.

Nor do we overlook the distinction that those who abandoned the Catholic Church when they were already baptized believers should do a humbler penance than those who were never in it before. Nor are they admitted to the clergy, whether they were rebaptized by the heretics, or had been received earlier and then went back to them, or were clergy or laity among them. And those of our people who are careless about these things, and perhaps make such people clergy in the Catholic Church or allow them to remain so, though they are rightly reproved by the more careful in brotherly fashion, still do not themselves think that clerical office should be conferred on any but those whom they know, or believe, to have been corrected of those evils. So all those who separate themselves from the Catholic Church's unity by a heinous crime slander her in vain. For, to use the apostle's words instead, "the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all the ungodliness and unrighteousness of men who hold the truth captive in unrighteousness." Unless they correct themselves, this wrath will find these men too, who hold the truth of Christian baptism captive in the unrighteousness of their sacrilegious separation.

But the Catholic Church, which, as was foretold of her, is spread through all nations with abundant fruitfulness, never corrects anyone's iniquity in such a way as to destroy in him the truth that belongs not to him but to her Lord. Why, then, does this man cry out so freely and confidently: "I baptized without misgiving the man whom you, sacrilegious one, had defiled; I baptized him, I say; I did what the apostle Paul did"? Let him read where the apostle Paul did this. And if he wants it understood of those men at Ephesus, then let him dare to say that John, a sacrilegious man, had defiled them. If he does not dare to say this, since it is the most obvious wickedness, let him at last stop stirring up fogs of false likeness out of a matter that is very different.

Then he adds the case of Agrippinus, bishop of Carthage, of the renowned martyr Cyprian, and of Cyprian's seventy predecessors, because they did this and ordered it to be done. How detestable is the error of men who think it praiseworthy to imitate certain things that famous men did wrongly, while they are strangers to those men's virtues! In the same way some would like to be compared with the apostle Peter if they deny Christ, and if they also compel the Gentiles to live like Jews, they aspire to be called his true brothers. These things were blameworthy in that great man, but the apostolic grace in him shone out so greatly that they were at once wiped away. No Christian of our times, not even a bishop, who has neither denied Christ nor compelled the Gentiles to live like Jews, can be ranked above him; I will not say that, but he cannot even be put on a level with him or come close to him in comparison. So too with the most glorious martyr Cyprian. If he refused to recognize the baptism of Christ given among heretics or schismatics, because he loathed too much those whom he grieved to see separated from the catholic unity he loved so dearly, his merits were so great, reaching all the way to the triumph of martyrdom, that this shadow was put to flight by the light of the charity in which he excelled. And so that the fruitful branch might become more fruitful still, whatever he had that needed pruning was removed, if by nothing else, then certainly by the final pruning-knife of his passion. Nor are we better than Cyprian because we acknowledge the truth of baptism even in the wickedness of heretics rather than deny it, just as we are not better than Peter because we do not compel the Gentiles to live like Jews. This is my reply concerning Agrippinus and the other bishops who are said to have held those councils. They held different views, yet they remained in unity with those whose opinion on this question differed from theirs, where charity covers a multitude of sins. For to men walking in this way in the truth of the Church, which they had reached, God could, as the apostle says, reveal even that in which they thought otherwise. The question was new at the time: how heretics were to be received. Its very novelty disturbed some brethren who rightly and fiercely detested the ruin of heresy, so that they believed that even the good which the heretics held to their own harm was to be condemned in them. To put briefly what I think on this matter: rebaptizing heretics, which those men are said to have done, was then a human error; but rebaptizing catholics, which these men still do, is always a presumption of the devil.

But I want this man to solve a problem for me. When he listed the bishops of the Roman church in order, he also mentioned Stephen among those whom he acknowledged to have held their episcopate unblemished. Now Stephen not only did not rebaptize heretics, but even judged that those who did so, or who decreed that it should be done, ought to be excommunicated, as the letters of other bishops and of Cyprian himself show. Yet Cyprian remained in the peace of unity with him. What will they say to that? Let them rack their wits as much as they can and consider whether they are able to answer. Look: there were two men at the same time, to say nothing of others, who held different views. They were two bishops of the most eminent churches, namely Rome and Carthage: Stephen and Cyprian, both established in catholic unity. Stephen held that the baptism of Christ was not to be repeated in anyone and was gravely angered at those who did it; Cyprian, on the other hand, thought that those baptized in heresy or schism should be baptized in the catholic Church, as not having the baptism of Christ. Many agreed with Cyprian, some with Stephen, and both remained in unity with them all. Now these men say, and use it to assert or excuse the cause of their separation, that in one communion of the sacraments the wicked stain the good, and that we must therefore withdraw by bodily separation from contact with the wicked, lest all perish alike. If that is true, then we must admit that the Church had already perished in the times of Stephen and Cyprian, and that none was left for those who came after, in which Donatus himself could be spiritually born. If they judge this a wicked thing to say, as indeed it is, then the Church remained from those times down to the times of Caecilian and Majorinus, or Donatus. Those who, according to these men, were admitted into it without baptism, full of all their sins and crimes, could not destroy it by staining it, and Cyprian and those who thought as he did about baptism made no division from their communion, because they did not believe that they could be stained by the sins of others in the unity and communion of Christ's sacraments. In the same way, then, the Church could also continue afterward. Growing, as was foretold of it, throughout the whole world, it could in no way be stained by the sins of others, of any traitors or criminals whatever, just as on one threshing floor the grain cannot be stained by the chaff until the time of winnowing, and just as within one net the bad fish swimming alongside the good do not destroy them until the time they reach the shore.

There was no reason, then, but only the greatest madness, in these men's separating themselves from the unity of Christ, which is spread throughout the whole world, on the pretext of avoiding communion with the wicked. Unless perhaps they distinguish crime from crime by some marvelous art, producing rules for their distinctions not from the Scriptures but from their own hearts, and saying that in the unity of sacramental communion other people's other crimes may be tolerated without contamination, but that everyone who shares the sacraments with such people is held fast by the crime of handing over the Scriptures. But it is superfluous to argue about this at length, especially since they very rarely dare to say it. They too are ashamed and feel that they are talking nonsense, and when they do say it, they make no attempt to support it with any divine testimony. What they usually have on their lips, when they accuse some people of others' sins in order to excuse the wickedness of their own separation, are texts like these: "When you saw a thief, you ran along with him"; "Do not share in the sins of others"; "Depart, go out from there, and touch nothing unclean"; "Whoever touches what is polluted is polluted"; "A little leaven corrupts the whole lump"; and others of the kind. In these the crime of handing over is not distinguished from other crimes by any special feature; rather, association with every sin is forbidden. Yet if Cyprian had understood these divine testimonies or precepts as these men do, he would certainly have separated himself from Stephen and not remained with him in the communion of catholic unity. For, according to the view about baptism which these men think must be held, Stephen, by admitting into the Church heretics and schismatics who, as they suppose, did not have baptism, was sharing in the sins of others, since the sins of those who had not been washed in true baptism certainly remained in them. Cyprian therefore ought to have withdrawn from his communion, so as not to run along with a thief, not to share in the sins of others, not to be defiled by contact with the unclean, not to become polluted by touching what was polluted, not to be corrupted by other people's leaven. Since he did not do this but remained in unity with them, the whole lump of that unity was then corrupted, and the Church did not survive to give birth later to these men's saints, Majorinus and Donatus. Since they in no way dare to say this, it remains for them to admit that the good remained with the wicked in the communion of the Christian sacraments without any stain of their own, and that the Church of Christ continued down to the time of Caecilian, not without any wicked people, as if already stored in the granary, but still on the threshing floor, mixed with chaff. In the same way, then, it could also continue afterward, as indeed it does continue, until it is winnowed and cleansed on the last day of judgment.

What, then, is the meaning of this great madness of theirs in separating from the unity of the body of Christ, which, as we read it was prophesied and now see fulfilled, is spreading throughout the whole world and among all nations? Here surely, as it is written, the wicked son calls himself righteous, but does not wash away his going out; that is, he does not excuse it, does not clear it, does not defend it, though in schismatic madness he did not fear to go out from the house of God into the plague of heresy. For if he were truly righteous, he would remain in the Church of Christ without any stain on himself, alongside those whom he either knew or thought to be unrighteous, as the apostle Paul did with the false brethren over whom he groans in his letters, and as Cyprian did with those whom he believed to be without baptism and full of their past sins, and whom he knew Stephen was admitting into the Church. He would not abandon the good because of the wicked, but would rather bear with the wicked for the sake of the good, enduring the threshing like grain with the chaff through the weight of charity, not yielding to the breezes even before the winnowing like the lightest dust. Persevering in this way in catholic unity, even with the wicked, whom these nets must necessarily hold until they reach the shore, he would still not run along with a thief, nor share in the sins of others, nor be stained by handling anyone's uncleanness, nor be polluted by touching what was polluted, nor be corrupted by anyone's leaven. For these things happen by consenting to sins, the way the serpent, through the woman, deceived the first man even in the happiness of paradise; not by communion in the sacraments, in which the unclean Judas could not contaminate his clean fellow disciples. The good, moreover, even now while still on the threshing floor and not yet in the granary, already withdraw and separate themselves from the wicked with whom they share the sacraments of God, by difference of conduct, not by bodily segregation; by living differently, not by going off to other conventicles. In this way they neither become one with the wicked nor depart from the unity of the Church.

Why, then, do they exaggerate to us the crime of some traitors or other, whom they have never been able to convict? But if we defend those men against their slanders, we will seem to be pleading the cause of certain individuals, not of the Church. Wherever and whoever the traitors were, Stephen, according to these men, was admitting into the Church not only the sin of traitors but also that of the very men who compelled them to hand over the Scriptures, and of absolutely all criminals, the shameful and the sacrilegious. For if those he admitted did not have baptism, all the sins, however grave and horrible, that they had committed remained in them and held them guilty without any remission. Such men Stephen admitted; with such men Cyprian was in catholic unity; and yet the Church did not perish but continued. Therefore the sins of others do not stain anyone in its unity. In vain did the wicked son hurry to leave his father's household; in vain does he call himself righteous, but does not wash away his going out. Or perhaps they will say that those whom Stephen admitted in this way were cleansed by sharing in that very unity, since charity covers a multitude of sins? If only they would say it! For we say this too, when we either urge or admonish them to return to unity. But on these terms no question about baptism will remain between us any longer. For if those baptized among heretics or schismatics are cleansed by the charity of unity itself when they come to the Church, then they are certainly rebaptized for no reason.

You see, then, how much this man has said in our favor in the speech to which you wanted me to reply. What need is there now for us to refute the charges he has brought against the bishops of the Roman church, whom he has attacked with incredible slanders? He accuses Marcellinus and his presbyters Miltiades, Marcellus and Sylvester of the crime of handing over the divine books and of offering incense. But are they therefore convicted, or shown to have been convicted by any solid documentary proof? He says they were wicked and sacrilegious; I answer that they were innocent. Why should I labor to prove my defense, when he has not made even a feeble attempt to prove his accusation? If there is any humanity in human affairs, I think we could more justly be blamed if we believed unknown men to be guilty rather than innocent when their enemies accuse them but prove their crime by no testimony. For even if the truth should perhaps be otherwise, what is due to humanity itself is certainly paid when one human being does not rashly suspect anything evil of another and does not readily believe anyone who accuses, since a man who brings a charge without a witness and without any documentary evidence shows himself to be a slanderous railer rather than a truthful accuser.

Add to this that Caecilian was pronounced innocent with Miltiades, then bishop of the Roman church, presiding, at the order of the emperor Constantine, to whom the accusers of Caecilian, bishop of the church of Carthage, had referred the whole case through the proconsul Anulinus. When these men's forebears, with most importunate obstinacy, complained to that emperor about this judgment, saying that it had not been fully or properly examined and delivered, they said nothing about Miltiades having handed over the Scriptures or offered incense. Yet they surely ought not even to have come to his hearing; they should rather have pointed out to the emperor beforehand, or pressed for it to be pointed out, that they ought not to plead their case before a man who had handed over the divine books and been defiled by sacrifices to idols. Since, then, they neither pointed this out beforehand nor thought it worth raising even when, defeated and angry, the judgment had gone against them in favor of Caecilian, why do these empty men now string together slanders so late in the day? Is it as if to darken Caecilian's innocence by discoloring the judge Miltiades, and to darken the Roman church itself, where they could neither condemn anyone by any judgment of theirs nor install one of their own, so to speak, in place of the man they had condemned? Against that church they at first used to send, secretly and from far away, visiting agents to the very few Africans of their party, agents whom this man was not ashamed to mention by name, until they ordained for the deceived little flock what passed for their own bishops. Indeed, after Caecilian had been cleared, they accused Felix, bishop of Aptunga, before the emperor, claiming that he was a most manifest traitor and that Caecilian therefore could not be a bishop, because he had been ordained by that traitor. Constantine did not refuse a hearing even to this accusation of theirs, though he had found them to be slanderers in the fabricated charges against Caecilian, and so he ordered that the case of Felix be examined. It was examined in Africa by the proconsul Aelian, and Felix too was declared innocent. The proconsular records survive; anyone who wishes may take them up and read them. This serves not only to crown the proof of Caecilian's innocence, to clear Felix himself most evidently, and to expose the slanders of those who had called him the fountain of all evils in their council. It also leads us to conclude that the life of Miltiades was perfectly pure of their accusations. Unless perhaps someone is so foolish as to believe that, since they did not spare Felix, by whom Caecilian had been ordained, they could have spared Miltiades, by whom he had been acquitted, if any rumor whatever had found fault with that bishop's life, even if no wound of conscience had [?] it. Or would they bring a charge about what they had invented concerning the forum of Aptunga, and keep silent about what had been done on the Capitol of the Romans?

As for Mensurius, what answer should I give? In his time, right up to the day of his death, no part of the people of unity was split off, and the very letters of Secundus of Tigisis, in which he is said to have been rebuked, confirm that they wrote to each other peaceably and remained in collegial fellowship. And when he chose to speak also about the church of Cirta, and assailed with what abuse he liked the catholic bishops there, what else did he achieve but to show clearly, by reviling holy men of our own time, well known to us, what we ought to think also about the unknown men whom he abuses in the same way? So then, if Profuturus, who died only a very few years ago, and Fortunatus, who is still in the body and succeeded him as bishop, were Manichees, then those men were traitors too: men far removed from our times and quite unknown, whom they never cease to accuse. Yet even their life is now very well known to us to be free of these men's slurs.

It is certainly no small and no inglorious consolation to any of us to be accused by the enemies of the Church together with the Church itself. Yet the Church's defense does not consist in defending the men whom these people attack by name with false accusations. Whatever Marcellinus, Marcellus, Sylvester, Miltiades, Mensurius, Caecilian and the others were, against whom they bring whatever charges they like in support of their dissent, they create no prejudice against the catholic Church spread throughout the whole world. We are in no way crowned by their innocence, and in no way condemned by their wickedness. If they were good, they were cleansed like grain in the threshing of the catholic threshing floor; if they were wicked, they were crushed like straw in the threshing of the catholic threshing floor. Within this threshing floor both good and wicked can be; outside it the good cannot be. Whoever is separated from this unity by the wind of pride, like chaff alone, why does he slander the Lord's threshing floor because of the chaff mixed in it?

We too say, and not only say but prove by the written records of the Church and the state, that Secundus of Tigisis, at whose assembled council they claim Caecilian was condemned, granted peace to confessed traitors so that there would be no schism, when the crime of handing over had been charged against him too by Purpurius of Limata. We say that Victor of Rusicade, Donatus of Calama, Donatus of Mascula, Marinus of Aquae Tibilitanae and Silvanus of Cirta were traitors, and that these same men were, as it were, the most severe condemners of traitors. This we prove by ecclesiastical, municipal and judicial records. But not all in the party of Donatus are traitors because these men were in it, nor is the party of Donatus innocent if these men should be shown innocent of the wickedness of handing over. For we would rather listen to Holy Scripture than either slander anyone over the sins of others or fear any similar slander ourselves. For "the soul that sins, it shall die," and "each one shall bear his own burden," and "whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment not on another but on himself." Both are allowed to grow until the harvest, lest when the weeds are gathered before the time, the wheat be uprooted with them. Goats and lambs graze mingled together in the best pastures until they are separated by the shepherd who cannot err. The nets of unity are filled with fish of every kind until they are brought to the judgment of the shore. The exception is that these men prejudge their own case by their perverse and false opinion, when they say they have justly separated themselves from the communion of the Christian world because of the sins of others. By this absurd and insane opinion they themselves bring it about that the sins of some of their members are charged to them all. If they think this just, then all of them are guilty of any most manifest crime found in a single person among them. But if they recognize that this is unjust, as it is, then all of them are guilty of a most wicked separation.

Now, since in this discourse the question concerns above all the one baptism, let our argument conclude where it began. In the very unity of the Lord's threshing floor the wicked are not to be praised because of the good, nor the good abandoned because of the wicked. In a single person, likewise, his perversity is not to be accepted because of what is sound in him, nor ought his soundness to be denied because of what is perverse in him. For the truth of the resurrection of the dead is held in the wickedness of the Jews; the truth of the one God who made the world is held in the wickedness of the Gentiles; in the wickedness of those who scatter because they do not gather with Christ is held the truth by which they drive out an unclean spirit in his name; in the wickedness of sacrilegious temples was found the truth by which they worshiped an unknown god; and in the wickedness of demons was found the truth by which they confessed Christ. So too the truth found in the wickedness of heretics, by which the sacrament of baptism is held, is not to be denied.
(p. 172, line 9, Knöll's edition). On the One Baptism, against Petilian, to Constantine: one book.

At that time a friend of mine received a book on the one baptism from some Donatist presbyter or other, who said that Petilian, their bishop of Constantina, had written it. My friend brought it to me and urged me strongly to answer it. I wanted my own book, in which I replied, to bear the same title as well, that is, On the One Baptism.

In that book I said that when the Donatists brought charges against Felix of Abthugni, who had ordained Caecilian, the Emperor Constantine did not refuse them the chance to accuse him, even though he had already found them to be slanderers who had made up charges against Caecilian. When the order of events was examined later, it was found to be otherwise. For the emperor first had Felix's case heard by the proconsul, and the record shows that Felix was acquitted there. Only afterwards did the emperor himself hear Caecilian together with his accusers and find him innocent, and that was when he found them to be slanderers in their charges against him. This order of events, established by the dates of the consuls, refutes and utterly overturns the slanders of the Donatists in that case far more forcefully, as we have shown elsewhere.
This book begins thus: "To respond to those who hold contrary views."
